comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for constructive feedback.

> The set of metrics is relatively narrow. How does this look on non-binary metrics? 

We have focused on binary accuracy because this is the metric of choice for many available routing benchmark datasets. For instance, the EmbedLLM dataset includes the popular MMLU, GSM8K (reasoning), and MBPP (coding) datasets, all of which can be evaluated with binary accuracy. Similarly, the recent SPROUT dataset (Somerstep et al., 2025) focuses on accuracy. 

However, UniRoute allows for a general loss function (see Eq. 1), and in fact on the RouterBench dataset, the ground-truth label is a continuous score from 0 to 1. Consistent with other datasets, we observe that UniRoute performs well on RouterBench (see Fig 2).

___


> It is unclear how robust this is to shifts in distribution compared to the validation set

We agree this is of interest, and in fact **Appendix G.4** presents one such study of distribution shift. Here, the LLM representations are computed on the Chatbot Arena prompts (online conversation prompts from real traffic), and UniRoute is tested on EmbedLLM (mostly Q&A prompts). The labels on the two datasets are also of different types. We demonstrate that UniRoute (K-Means) is able to outperform K-NN despite these challenging shifts in the prompts and labels.

Please also see a longer response to a related question *“Limited robustness reporting”* from Reviewer fvKV.
___

> How stable is the cost-tuning knob across datasets and model pools? 

We presume that by “cost-tuning knob”, the reviewer is referring to $\\lambda$ in Eq 6. Note that there is a correspondence between $B$ (average cost upper bound) in Eq 5, and $\\lambda$ in Eq 6. In particular, the larger $\\lambda$, the smaller the average cost. See also the detailed response on this point to Reviewer 44vL.

Since the average cost clearly depends on the dataset, **the same $\\lambda$ may not yield the same average cost across datasets**. In our work, we sweep this parameter to produce a deferral curve for evaluating routers (see Fig 3 and Fig 6 in the Appendix). In other words, $\\lambda$ is a quality-cost trade-off parameter that must be chosen on a per-application basis. Sweeping a quality-cost trade-off parameter to produce such a trade-off curve is standard in the literature of model routing (see, for instance, Somerstep
et al., 2025, and Hu et al., 2024b).

We reiterate that we only need to train once (i.e., to estimate the expected loss of each LLM $\\mathbb{E}_{y|x}[\\ell(x, y, h^{(m)})]$ in Eq 6), after which we can adjust $\\lambda$ post hoc.
___


> Are there subgroups or adversarial examples which can reduce performance? 

Thanks for the interesting question, which we fully agree would be a fruitful avenue for future work. Indeed, there is recent work studying the robustness of LLM routing to adversarial inputs: Shafran et al., *“Rerouting LLM Routers”*, arXiV 2025. Further studying how these interplay with cluster-based routing would be of considerable interest. We will add a pointer in the discussion on future work.


> Is it possible to combine this with a learned router for seen models to get improvements when comparing to a static pool?

Thanks for the suggestion, which we agree is very interesting to explore. Leveraging model-identity based parameters for those which are in the training set (and model-feature based parameters for those which are not) would roughly mirror hybrid cold- and warm-start methods for matrix factorisation based collaborative filtering. A key challenge here is designing a suitable mechanism to gracefully fall back on model-feature based parameters for those models not observed in training (e.g., via a prior or regulariser on the model-identity based parameters, per Agarwal and Chen, *“Regression-based latent factor models”*, KDD 2009). We will add a pointer in the discussion on future work.

> Q1. Can you add results or at least a justified comparison against the most recent approach(es) that use a similar intermediate representation?

To our knowledge, **we are not aware of existing works that rely on similar LLM embeddings for dynamic routing**. The two most related works are Zhuang et al., 2024 (EmbedLLM, static routing), and Li 2025 (LLM Bandit, RL-based approach). We compare UniRoute to both of these methods in our experiments.

## Compared to EmbedLLM:

While EmbedLLM performs LLM embedding, the way we embed LLMs is very different from this approach. In EmbedLLM, a router is trained to predict the per-prompt quality metric of each LLM using a training dataset with correctness labels, with one prediction head per LLM. The weights of the prediction heads (i.e., matrix of size #embedding dimension x #models) are directly used as LLM embeddings. 

Two crucial differences to our proposal are:

1. EmbedLLM requires correctness labels on the training prompts to define LLM representations. Our proposed representation is based on clustering and is applicable even in the absence of labeled prompts.


2. **EmbedLLM does not natively support dynamic routing, without full retraining**. Furthermore, in EmbedLLM, the embedding of each LLM depends on the (static) LLM pool. That is, adding or removing other LLMs from the pool can change the embedding of an LLM. Our proposal does not suffer from this disadvantage.

The Retrained MatrixFactorization (MatFac) baseline in Figure 2 is the closest adaptation of the EmbedLLM approach to dynamic routing.

## Compared to LLM Bandit:

In LLM Bandit, the representation of an LLM is the parameter vector of a feedforward network. For each LLM, the parameter is optimized so that the network can predict the correctness score of the LLM given an input prompt. However:

1. **Adding a new LLM thus involves an expensive gradient-based training procedure.**  While Li 2025 also proposed an efficient procedure that requires only 50 prompts, the procedure involves counting the number of LLMs in the current pool that can correctly respond to each prompt in a training set.

2. The above also means that the representation of the (M+1)-th LLM will necessarily depend on the M models in the current pool. In other words, **the order in which LLMs arrive in the pool influence the learned identity vectors of future LLMs**. Our proposed LLM representation is computationally efficient. Moreover, in our proposal, LLM representations are computed independently of each other (i.e., not a function of the order of LLMs).

A quantitative comparison to Li 2025 is presented in Appendix I.1, where we compare against the numbers reported in Fig 3b of Li 2025. Unfortunately, there is **no source code released by Li 2025**, and their approach involves a **complex pipeline, making it challenging to faithfully reproduce their results without their implementation**. To elaborate, the approach first requires training model identity vectors (i.e., LLM representation) via iterative gradient updates. Then, a routing policy network is *pre-trained* on various data sources by consuming the model identity vectors as input. Lastly, the policy network is further trained with reinforcement learning (involving PPO, mixup regularization, and the use of a Beta prior on some learnable weights). See Sec C (appendix) in Li 2025.
_____

> Q2. Ablation depth: If you ablate the proposed module but keep the training data / hyperparams the same, how much of the gain remains? This would confirm it’s not just better tuning.

We would appreciate further detail regarding the preferred ablation study. For example, the number of clusters $K$ is a hyper-parameter we tune for our methods. Would you like to see a comparison between UniRoute (K-Means) and UniRoute (LearnedMap) variants of our method with $K$ kept fixed?

Please note that we propose a procedure to select the best $K$ by validating the performance of each candidate $K$ with the area under the deferral curve (see Appendix G.2). This is done for both the number of clusters $K$ in UniRoute and the number of neighbors $K$ in $K$-NN. The number of hidden nodes in “Retrained MLP” and “Retrain MatFac” is also chosen by the same procedure.
_____

I thank the authors for the detailed and thoughtful responses to my comments. The clarifications regarding the cluster sensitivity and the discussion on how the method could be extended to settings with noisy or missing labels were helpful. I also appreciate the expanded explanation of the bilinear form and the discussion of alternatives such as MLP-based architectures. I think that the additional comment regarding this would be beneficial for the paper.

Overall, the rebuttal addresses my concerns, and I will maintain my positive rating.

summary.value: The paper studies routing among multiple LLMs when the model pool can change after training. The idea is to fingerprint each model by taking its error to a validation set, giving us a way to then route promots to a cluster and let us estimate which model will do best. They cover two approaches, one which is K-means clusters and one which is a learned assignment. This produces budget-and-quality frontier improvements over baselines on a range of benchmarks and models.

2. The test-time approach is amenable to many real use cases

summary.value:
This paper tackles dynamic model routing for LLM serving: at test time, the pool of available LLMs can change , so retraining a router every time is impractical. The proposed solution, UniRoute, “fingerprints” each LLM using its error pattern on a validation set, and routes prompts using a prompt embedding + a model embedding, with a cost–quality trade-off controlled by a Lagrange-style parameter. Empirically, they show improved cost–accuracy frontiers over dynamic baselines (e.g., k-NN / retraining-style approaches) across multiple routing benchmarks, including settings with many unseen models.

The authors provides a comprehensive rebuttal and all reviewers agreed on the acceptance of this paper.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the importance of dynamic routing, and for constructive feedback.

> Q1. Prop 1: If I understand correctly, the Lagrangian multiplier \lambda  is specific to an instance of x and H, while h is the distribution of . Therefore, denoting this multiplier as …  is confusing. Please correct me if I am wrong.

**There appears to be a misunderstanding.** We would like to clarify that in Prop 1, $\\lambda$ is **not** specific to an input instance of $x$, or a specific set of LLMs $\\mathcal{H}$. In particular, we **do not require the budget constraint to hold for each input instance $x$**. Instead, we require the expected cost (over instances $x$ and LLMs $\\mathcal{H}$) to be in budget. As a result, the Lagrange multiplier is specific to the cost budget $B$ (in Eq 5), and the meta-distribution that generates the set of LLMs. 

Please see our answers to the following points for further elaboration.

To elaborate, using the same notation as in the submission, we write $\\mathfrak{H}$ to denote the meta-distribution that generates a set of LLMs $\\mathcal{H}$ (see lines 153-161). In the optimization problem in Eq 5, we seek to find a router (i.e., **a function**) that minimizes the expected loss, subject to the constraint that the expected cost is upper-bounded by $B$. Importantly, the expectations in Eq 5 are also over $\\mathcal{H}$ (treated as a random set).

Prop 1 states that given $B$, there exists a $\\lambda_\\mathfrak{H}$ such that the optimal router $r^\*$ to Eq 5 is given in Eq 6. Note that $\\lambda_\\mathfrak{H}$ does not depend on one instance of $\\mathcal{H}$ because we consider an average over sets of LLMs. This is why $\\lambda_\\mathfrak{H}$ depends on the meta-distribution $\\mathfrak{H}$.
____



> Q2.1. Implication of Prop 1: the optimal  r* for Eq 5 is the minimizer to Eq 6 for some \lambda. However, it does not mean that optimizing over  \lambda and Eq 6 is going to give us the optimal  r* for Eq 5. 

If we understand correctly, the reviewer is of the view that the optimal router $r*$ uses an instance-dependent $\\lambda$. As we have clarified above, the optimal $r*$ in Prop 1 does not use an instance-dependent $\\lambda$. 

Recall from the above that given $B$, there exists a $\\lambda_\\mathfrak{H}$ such that the optimal router $r^\*$ to Eq 5 is given in Eq 6. For brevity we write $\\lambda$ for $\\lambda_\\mathfrak{H}$. Eq .6 gives the functional form of this optimal function $r^\*$.

Eq 6:

$$\\underset{m \\in[ | \mathscr{H} | ]}{\\arg \\min} \\mathbb{E}_{y | x}[\\ell(x, y, h^{(m)})]  + \\lambda \\cdot c( h^{(m)} )$$

*  $\\mathbb{E}\_{y \mid x} [ \ell(x, y,h^{(m)}) ] $   is the expected loss incurred by the LLM $h^{(m)}$ on the query $x$;
*  $c( h^{(m)} )$ is the cost of running $h^{(m)}$ on a query.

Eq 6 means, at test time, given a test query $x$, we pick the LLM with the lowest cost-adjusted expected loss, where the expected loss is to be estimated as described in Sections 5.1 and 5.2. We stress that **the presence of argmin in Eq 6 does *not* mean that we perform a local optimization of $\\lambda$ for each $x$**. The presence of argmin (over candidate models) is a result of a mathematical derivation (see proof in Appendix C.2).
____

> Q2.2. Therefore, the suggestion of tuning $\lambda$, while being something sensible to do, is simply ignoring Prop 1….

We understand that the reviewer is referring to lines 184-185 which state

> > If one wishes to sweep $B$ to trace a cost-quality deferral curve (Appendix F.2), one may equally treat $\\lambda$ as a tunable constant.

In practice, we are interested in evaluating a router by quantifying the average quality against the average cost. This is achieved by plotting the “deferral curve”. This is also what existing works consider (see Hu et al., 2024b, Somerstep et al., 2025, for instance). The negation of the objective in Eq 5 is the average quality, and the average cost is the left-hand side of the constraint.

In principle, we can plot the deferral curve by repeatedly solving Eq 5 for different values of $B$. However, as established by Prop 1, there is a correspondence between $B$ in Eq 5 and $\\lambda$ in Eq 6. So, we may equally sweep $\\lambda$ in Eq 6. This is how we plot the deferral curves in Fig 3 (and Fig 6 in the appendix). The advantage of the latter approach is that we only need to estimate $x \mapsto \\mathbb{E}_{y | x}[\\ell(x, y, h^{(m)})]$ in Eq 6 once, and simply use Eq 6 with a plug-in estimator.  

We will make this clearer.
____

We thank the reviewer for recognizing the novelty of our work.

> The given clustering-based examples rely on the representativeness of the validation dataset. While this works, the paper gives limited insight into sensitivity. What happens if clusters are not well aligned with the task structure?

As the reviewer correctly notes, UniRoute performs best when the clusters are aligned with the underlying tasks. However, we observed that **UniRoute can still be performant even when there is no clear task structure**. For instance, this is the case for the Headlines dataset where all prompts are about news related to finance. See Fig 2 in the maintext, and Fig 6c in the appendix.

It is also interesting to note that UniRoute (K-Means) does not perform as well as UniRoute (LearnedMap) in this case. This is because UniRoute (K-Means) assumes that the average error of an LLM on the cluster a query belongs to is a good estimate of the error on the query itself. If there is a clear structure, then UniRoute (K-Means) offers a simple and effective dynamic routing strategy. If there is no clear cluster structure, then UniRoute (LearnedMap) is more appropriate because an input query is soft-assigned (via softmax) to multiple clusters, and a weighted combination of per-cluster errors is used to estimate the per-query error.
____


> The proposed method assumes that you have access to a validation dataset with labels. How could this be generalized to noisy labels for a validation dataset or a validation dataset without labels?

Thanks for the interesting question. Without explicit labels, one would have to rely on reasonable proxies to these labels. For example, if the LLM’s output probabilities are well calibrated, one could use the per-cluster average log-likelihood.

We emphasise however that it is fairly typical for there to be _some_ labelled samples for a new LLM, even if in the form of standard benchmark datasets. 
____


> UniRoute represents the performance of the new LLM via the bilinear form . Can you explain why the bilinear form is expressive enough to model the interaction between prompts and models? Can there be more complex models that uses  and  as input features and estimates the performance?

This is a great question. Our motivation for the bilinear form was simply that it is a natural generalisation of the standard model identity based routing, wherein one could interpret the model embedding as a one-hot vector.

Nonetheless, one could indeed consider forms other than the bilinear similarity between prompt and model embeddings. For example, one could concatenate the two embeddings, and feed them into an MLP. Our early experiments with such models did not demonstrate significant benefits over the bilinear form. Nonetheless, such forms could be useful in other settings, and could be worth further study. We will add a comment.

____

summary.value: The paper studies LLM routing under dynamic model pools, where test-time available LLMs may differ from training-time ones. It proposes UniRoute, which learns a bilinear scoring function γ(x, h) = Φ(x)ᵀΨ(h). Prompts are embedded (and clustered) once; LLMs are represented by their per-cluster error rates on a small validation set. Routing is then simple cost-adjusted argmin over any test-time pool. The paper gives a Bayes-optimal rule for the dynamic setting and an excess-risk bound for the cluster-based instantiation. Experiments on four public routing-style benchmarks with 30+ unseen LLMs show UniRoute outperforms strong dynamic baselines (ZeroRouter, K-NN) and avoids retraining costs.

strengths.value:
- Relevant problem: tackles a practical, current task where LLM/agent methods are still brittle, the problem choice is well motivated.
- The components fit together: the modeling choices are consistent with the objective, and the pipeline is implementable without exotic assumptions.
- Across multiple datasets/settings, the method shows consistent improvements over the stated baselines, not just one cherry-picked case.
- There is at least some attempt at digging into why it works (error breakdown / qualitative examples), which is better than many incremental papers.
- Reproducible direction: The paper uses mostly standard toolchains; another group should be able to re-implement this without reverse-engineering half the setup.

weaknesses.value:
- Ablations are thin: key modules are turned on/off only in one setting; we don’t see if the effect is stable across datasets/scales. A 2–3 row ablation table per main component would already help.
- Limited robustness reporting: no real stress test (distribution shift, noisier inputs, or lower-resource regime). Right now, the method looks tuned to a friendly setup.
- Clarity on compute/cost: method adds some overhead but the paper doesn’t quantify it clearly; for adoption, people will want to know the inference/training cost relative to the simplest baseline.

questions.value:
1. Can you add results or at least a justified comparison against the most recent approach(es) that use a similar intermediate representation? Right now the reader has to guess how your method would fare against them.
2. Ablation depth: If you ablate the proposed module but keep the training data / hyperparams the same, how much of the gain remains? This would confirm it’s not just better tuning.
3. Compute: What is the actual training cost (GPU-hours, model size) and inference latency delta vs. the strongest baseline?

comment.value:
> Q3. Compute: What is the actual training cost (GPU-hours, model size) and inference latency delta vs. the strongest baseline?

We consider the same experimental setting as in Fig 2 for the EmbedLLM dataset. We compare the wall time of our proposed *UniRoute (K-Means)* to the strongest baseline, which is *Retrained MLP* in this case. Note that all approaches studied in this work (including UniRoute) start from embedding queries with the Gecko embedding network. So, to minimize the variance in time measurement, we pre-compute Gecko embeddings and exclude this step from the following results.

Reporting time in seconds:



|Operation | UniRoute (K-Means) | Retrained MLP | 
|:---|:---:|---:|
| Training | 1.41 | 8.18 |
| Route one test example | $0.37 \times 10^{-3}$ | $3.19 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| Add a new LLM to the pool | $57.90 \times 10^{-3}$ | 8.18  |

For adding a new LLM to the pool, we exclude the time to run batch inference to generate responses for the prompts in the validation set because this is a common step for both approaches. 

We observe that UniRoute is faster than Retrained MLP for both training and inference. In fact, it is also better in terms of quality (see Fig 2). Since Retrained MLP does not support dynamic routing, adding a new LLM to the pool requires retraining the router (hence the same wall time for training and for adding a new LLM). By contrast, UniRoute only requires estimating per-cluster errors of the new LLM. Unlike the MLP approach, this does not require any expensive gradient updates. The above wall time is consistent with the runtime complexity analysis in Appendix H.2.

We make the following additional remarks.

1. We emphasize that the above **K-means clustering uses a much larger dataset compared to MLP**. This is because K-Means clustering (training) requires only unlabeled input queries, whereas the MLP router requires labeled queries. Requiring no labels allows one to easily afford a large set of training queries. In the above experiment, the **UniRoute uses 18k unlabeled examples, whereas Retrained MLP uses 3k labeled (validation) examples**. Recall from Sec 4.1 that we consider the setting where the validation set (i.e., containing labels from test LLMs) is limited.

2. The above latency analysis is in an illustrative setting where the query embedding network (i.e., Gecko in this case) is frozen. In reality, **we expect router retraining to take much longer if the query embedder is also trained**. In such a case, Retrained MLP would incur a significant cost every time the LLM pool changes. Our UniRoute approach would require backbone training only once.

3. Inference latency and training time are only one aspect of the overall cost when deploying a router. In practice, there are engineering and maintenance costs that one needs to take into consideration. 

4. There are many applications where **full router retraining is infeasible** either because smaller (open-sourced) models are released frequently, or because the number of possible subsets of LLMs one can use is exponentially large. Even if the underlying LLMs are fixed, **the test-time LLM pool can change frequently**. In particular, the exact pool of LLMs available to a user may vary, depending on e.g., the availability of GPUs for serving, LLM licensing requirements, suitability to the user’s particular task, etc. One can imagine use cases where custom-made LLMs of different sizes have to be updated frequently (e.g., LLM assistants for stock market news), and possibly on proprietary data (e.g., LLMs for internal documents of a large company). 
________

summary.value: This paper studies the problem of dynamic model routing for LLM inference: given a prompt and a pool of candidate LLMS of different cost, select the cheapest model that will still answer well, even when the candidate pool dynamically changes. Existing work mostly assumes a static pool, and retrains the router whenever a new model appears, which is impractical and expensive. The authors formalize routing with a dynamic pool and propose UniRoute, which represents each LLM as a feature vector using its prediction error on the validation dataset, and represents each input prompt via a learned embedding. Then, they estimate for each model and prompt pair the probability of error plus a cost term and pick the minimum. Two examples of UniRoute are presented; they are clustering-based routers where prompts are grouped into clusters learned using the training dataset. The authors argue that these are approximations to an optimal routing rule and provide an excess risk bound. Experimentally, the authors evaluate UniRoute against multiple baselines that cover static and dynamic routing methods on several public routing benchmarks. Empirically, UniRoute attains better cost accuracy tradeoff than baseline methods.

strengths.value:
- The paper addresses a realistic and under-explored setting. Most prior work focuses on a fixed pool of LLMs and require retraining when a new model is added, UniRoute explicitly designed to handle a dynamic pool of LLMs.
- To my knowledge, the solution proposed by the authors is novel and quite simplistic. I think that the cluster-based example setups are practical and easy to implement. It is also cost-effective to adapt to new models.
- The paper gives an explicit optimal routing rule that shows the tradeoff between the predicted error and the model cost via a Lagrangian multiplier. It also shows how UniRoute approximates that.

weaknesses.value:
- The given clustering-based examples rely on the representativeness of the validation dataset. While this works, the paper gives limited insight into sensitivity. What happens if clusters are not well aligned with the task structure? 
- The proposed method assumes that you have access to a validation dataset with labels. How could this be generalized to noisy labels for a validation dataset or a validation dataset without labels? (I think that an intuitive answer would be enough instead of running a whole set of experiments.)

questions.value:
- UniRoute represents the performance of the new LLM via the bilinear form $\Phi(x)^|\top\Psi(x)$. Can you explain why the bilinear form is expressive enough to model the interaction between prompts and models? Can there be more complex models that uses $\Phi(x)$ and $\Psi(x)$ as input features and estimates the performance?

- Line 330, "... incorrect predic let..."
- Line 386, missing "." at the end of the sentence.

comment.value:
> Q2.3 The main problem is that it is not clear whether the values of \lambda  satisfying Prop 1 can be found constructively.

We agree that given $B$, mathematically deriving the closed-form expression for the corresponding $\\lambda$ is challenging. Fortunately there is no need to derive $\\lambda$ because in practice it is common to evaluate a router by its deferral curve (see Fig 3), which involves sweeping $\\lambda$ as explained above. We only need the fact that there is a correspondence between $B$ and $\\lambda$. Note that Lemma 5 (appendix) guarantees that increasing $\\lambda$ will decrease the average cost. So, in practice, in a rare event where the specific $\\lambda$ corresponding to a given average cost is desired, then we may use a simple line search to find it.
____


> Q3. Unclear formulation in Sec 4: for simplicity, let $\\Phi \\in \\mathbb{R}^{|X| \times K}$,  $\\Psi \in \\mathbb{R}^{|H| \times K}$. Hence,  (I'm assuming the transpose in (9) is a typo).... From (8), I got the impression that the domain of  $\\gamma$ is $R_+$. Therefore, something about the current formulation does not add up.


**$\\gamma$ is indeed a scalar function, and the formulation in Section 4 is consistent with this**. At line 204, we have

>> $\\Phi: \\mathscr{X} \to \\mathbb{R}^K$ and $\\Psi: \\mathcal{H}_\\mathrm{all} \to \\mathbb{R}^K$.

Thus, $\\Phi$ and $\\Psi$ **are vector-valued functions, not matrices.** Concretely, $\\Phi$ takes an input query $x$ and produces a $K$-dimensional **column** vector representing the query. $\\Psi$ takes one LLM $h$ and also produces a $K$-dimensional column vector representing the LLM. The expression $\\Phi(x)^\top \\Psi(h)$ in Eq 9 denotes the dot product between two vectors $\\Phi(x)$ and $\\Psi(h)$, giving a real number. Please note that the transpose $^\\top$ is not a typo. The co-domain of $\\gamma$ in Eq 9 is $\\mathbb{R}$.
______


> Q4. Line 271: underperform vs what?

[Zhuang et al., 2024] observed that $K$-NN may underperform compared to their proposed Matrix Factorization approach. We will make this clearer. Note that this Matrix Factorization approach is referred to as “MatFac” in our experiments.
____


> Q5. Unclear motivation for clustering in Sec 5: What is the reason for clustering here? Is it only for computational efficiency?

To support a wide variety of LLMs, we think that it is simplest to represent each LLM as a fixed-length dense vector. As to why clustering, we are motivated by how humans compare different LLMs: evaluate them on a number of important tasks that can contrast their skills (e.g., reasoning, math). This viewpoint lends itself to treating each LLM as a vector of per-task performance metrics. However, directly applying this idea would require access to the task label for each query, which is often difficult to acquire. By contrast, clustering provides an efficient means to discover latent tasks. The proposed cluster-based approach is also computationally efficient. In particular, this requires **no expensive gradient update** and is a **one-off cost** for each LLM to be added to the pool. Further routing operations can operate entirely on this vector. 

Further, estimating errors at a per-cluster level can **reduce overfitting**. This is evident from the higher performance of UniRoute compared to Retrained MLP and Retrained MatFac (see Fig 2), which estimates per-query errors directly.
____

We thank the reviewer for recognizing the strength of our empirical results, and the importance of dynamic routing.


> Limited robustness reporting: no real stress test

A robustness study is presented in Appendix G.4, where **we evaluate UniRoute on a test set that follows a different distribution from the training prompts**. We train UniRoute on Chatbot Arena data where prompts are online conversation prompts, and test on EmbedLLM which contains mostly question answering prompts. The LLM representations are computed using Chatbot Arena prompts.

Besides shifts in prompt distribution, the labels on the two datasets are also of different types. Specifically, the labels in Chatbot Arena are pairwise comparison labels (through users’ voting), whereas labels in EmbedLLM are pointwise scores (i.e., there is a ground truth response for each prompt). In Fig 7 (appendix), we demonstrate that UniRoute (K-Means) is able to outperform $K$-NN despite these challenging shifts in the prompts and labels. Note that prompts in the Chatbot Arena are prompts “in the wild” from real traffic. See Zheng et al., 2023 for details of the dataset. **Chatbot Arena prompts may be seen as noisy inputs**, compared to prompts in standard benchmarks such as GSM8K, MMLU, for instance. GSM8K and MMLU are included in the EmbedLLM dataset.
_____


> Clarity on compute/cost: method adds some overhead but the paper doesn’t quantify it clearly.

Please see **Appendix H** for a detailed cost analysis of UniRoute and a simple router retraining baseline. One important conclusion is that there is a large difference in the costs of the two methods for adding a new LLM. In particular, the cost of adding a new LLM with UniRoute is independent of the training sample size, and the size of the current LLM pool. By contrast, retraining a router would depend on these quantities.
